    #Functions of Several Variables

    Equation of a Circle

    (x−a)2+(y−b)2=r2 where r>0

    Equation an an Ellipse

    α2α(x−a)2​+β2β(y−b)2​=1

    where α>0, β>0 and r>0

    Taking square root of the denominator gives the radius in the axis.

    Equation of a Plane

    ax+by+cz=d

    Coefficients make up the normal vector n=(a,b,c) to the plane

    Equation of a Sphere

    (x−a)2+(y−b)2+(z−c)2=r2 where r>0

    Equation of an Ellipsoid

    α(x−a)2+β(y−b)2+γ(z−c)2=r2

    where α>0, β>0, γ>0 and r>0

    #Partial Derivatives

    Definition of Partial Derivatives

    fx​(a.b)=t→alim​ t−af(t,b)−f(a,b)​

    Gradient Vectors

    ∇f(x,y)=(fx​,fy​,fz​)=∂x∂f​i+∂y∂f​j+∂z∂f​k

    Chain Rule

    w=f(x,y,z) where x(t), y(t) and z(t)

    dtdw​=∂x∂w​⋅dtdx​+∂y∂w​⋅dtdy​+∂z∂w​⋅dtdz​

    w=f(x,y) where x(s,t,u) and y(s,t,u)

    ∂s∂w​=∂x∂w​⋅∂s∂x​+∂y∂w​⋅∂s∂y​

    ∂t∂w​=∂x∂w​⋅∂t∂x​+∂y∂w​⋅∂t∂y​

    Implicit Differentiation

    z is defined as a function of x and y by an equation F(x,y,z)=const

    ∂x∂F​⋅∂x∂x​+∂y∂F​⋅∂x∂y​+∂z∂F​⋅∂x∂z​=0

    ∂x∂F​⋅1+∂y∂F​⋅0+∂z∂F​⋅∂x∂z​=0

    ∂x∂F​+∂z∂F​⋅∂x∂z​=0

    ∂x∂z​=Fz​−Fx​​

    #Gradient Vectors

    #Tangent Plane and Normal Line

    Equation of Tangent Plane to Level Surface F(x,y,z)

    ∇F(x0​, y0​, z0​)⋅(x−x0​ ,y−y0​, z−z0​)=0

    Fx​(x−x0​)+Fy​(y−y0​)+Fz​(z−z0​)=0

    ∂x∂F​(x−x0​)+∂y∂F​(y−y0​)+∂z∂F​(z−z0​)=0

    Equation of Normal Line to Level Surface F(x,y,z)

    r=(x0​, y0​, z0​)+t∇F(x0​, y0​, z0​)

    x=x0​+t∂x∂F​

    y=y0​+t∂y∂F​

    z=z0​+t∂z∂F​

    Equation of Tangent Plane to z=f(x,y)

    F(x,y,z)=0

    F(x,y,z)=f(x,y)−z

    ∇F⋅(x−x0​, y−y0​, z−z0​)=0

    (fx​, fy​, −1)⋅(x−x0​, y−y0​, z−z0​)=0

    fx​(x−x0​)+fy​(y−y0​)−(z−z0​)=0

    z=z0​+fx​(x−x0​)+fy​(y−y0​)

    z=f(x0​, y0​)+fx​(x−x0​)+fy​(y−y0​)

    z=f(x0​, y0​)+∇f⋅(x−x0​, y−y0​)

    #Linear Approximation and Total Differentials

    Linear Approximation

    f(x,y)≈f(a,b)+∇f(a,b)⋅(x−a, y−b)

    L(x,y)=f(a,b)+fx​(a,b)⋅(x−a)+fy​(a,b)⋅(y−b)

    Total Differentials

    L(x,y)=f(a,b)+fx​(a,b)⋅(x−a)+fy​(a,b)⋅(y−b)

    L(x,y)−f(a,b)=fx​(a,b)⋅(x−a)+fy​(a,b)⋅(y−b)

    L(a+Δx, b+Δy)−f(a,b)=fx​(a,b)⋅Δx+fy​(a,b)⋅Δy

    df=fx​(a,b)⋅Δx+fy​(a,b)⋅Δy

    df=∇f(a,b)⋅(Δx,Δy)

    Δf=f(a+Δx, b+Δy)−f(a,b)

    Δf≈L(a+Δx, b+Δy)−f(a,b)

    Δf≈df

    #Directional Derivatives and Max/Min Rate of Change

    Directional Derivatives

    Unit vector u=∣v∣v​

    Du​ f(x,y)=∇f(x,y)⋅u

    Du​ f(x,y)=fx​(x,y)u1​+fy​(x,y)u2​

    Maximum and Minimum Rate of Change

    At a point P(a,b), the directional derivative is the rate of change of f in the direction u.

    Du​ f(P)=∇f(P)⋅u

    Du​ f(P)=∣∇f(P)∣∣u∣cosθ

    Du​ f(P)=∣∇f(P)∣cosθ

    Since ∇f(P) is constant, the directional derivative is dependent on the angle θ.
    From observation, maximum value of Du​ f(P) is when cosθ=1, where θ=0.
    Maximum value is when u has the same direction as gradient vector ∇f(P)and
    minimum value is when cosθ=−1, where θ=π, and u is in the opposite direction.

    Dumax​​=∣∇f(P)∣

    umax​=∣∇f(P)∣∇f(P)​

    Dumin​​=−∣∇f(P)∣

    umin​=−∣∇f(P)∣∇f(P)​

    #Global and Local Extrema

    #Maximum, Minimum and Saddle Points

    A function has a global maximum and minimum when:

    • Function is continuous
    • Closed and bounded

    Local Extrema

    ∇f(a,b)=(0,0) where fx​=0 and fy​=0

    Singular point if either fx​=0 or fy​=0 does not exist

    Stationary point if both fx​=0 and fy​=0 exist

    Critical point if (a,b) is a singular or stationary point

    Saddle point if (a,b) is a stationary point but not a local maximum or minimum

    Second Derivative Test for Local Extrema

    D(a,b)=​fxx​fyx​​fxy​fyy​​​

    D(a,b)=fxx​⋅fyy​−fxy​2

    If D>0 and fxx​>0, then f(a,b) is a local minimum.

    If D>0 and fxx​<0, then f(a,b) is a local maximum.

    If D<0, then f(a,b) is a saddle point.

    If D=0, the test gives no information.

    The second derivative test is not applicable to functions of 3 or more variables.

    #Langrangian Function

    Langrangian Function

    L(x,y,λ)=f(x,y)−λ⋅g(x,y) subject to a constraint g(x,y)=0

    Lx​=fx​−λgx​=0

    Ly​=fy​−λgy​=0

    Lλ​=−g=0

    Langrange Multiplier for One Equality Constraint

    Find all values of x, y and λ such that ∇f(x,y)=λ∇g(x,y).

    g(x,y)=k is the constraint function. Evaluate f at all points (x,y) that are found.

    Largest of these values is the maximum while smallest of these values is the minimum.

    Langrange Multiplier for Two Equality Constraints

    L(x,y,z,λ,μ)=f(x,y,x)−λ⋅g(x,y,z)−μ⋅h(x,y,z)

    Type 1 Regions

    x is bounded between two constants — a and b.

    y is bounded between two functions of x — g(x).

    Type 2 Regions

    x is bounded between two functions of y — h(y).

    y is bounded between two constants — c and d.

    D={(x,y):c≤y≤d, h1​(y)≤x≤h2​(y)}

    ∬D​ f(x,y) dA=∫cd​∫h1​(y)h2​(y)​ f(x,y) dxdy

    #Sequences

    Definition of Limit of a Sequence

    The sequence {an​} converges to the number L if for every ϵ>0, there corresponds
    an integer N such that for all n, where n>N ⟶ ∣an​−L∣<ϵ. In other words,
    the value of an​ is within ϵ of L.

    Properties of Limits

    n→∞lim​ (C⋅an​)=C n→∞lim​ an​

    n→∞lim​ (an​±bn​)=n→∞lim​ an​±n→∞lim​ bn​

    n→∞lim​ (an​⋅bn​)=n→∞lim​ an​⋅n→∞lim​ bn​

    n→∞lim​ bn​an​​=n→∞lim​ bn​n→∞lim​ an​​ provided that n→∞lim​ bn​=0 and bn​=0 for all n

    Interchanging Limits

    n→∞lim​ sinn1​=sin(n→∞lim​ n1​)=sin0=0

    n→∞lim​ en1​=en→∞lim​ n1​=e0=1

    n→∞lim​ (n2+3n2​)3=(n→∞lim​ n2+3n2​)3=13=1

    n→∞lim​ n2+3n2​​=n→∞lim​ n2+3n2​​=1​=1

    Subsequences

    If n→∞lim​ an​=L, then every subsequence of {an​} converges to L.

    Squeeze Theorem

    n→∞lim​n!3n​= ?

    n!3n​=13​⋅23​⋅33​⋅43​...n−23​⋅n−13​⋅n3​

    Each subsequent term after the third is smaller than 1.

    Thus, the upper bound of the sequence is 13​⋅23​⋅33​⋅n3​=2n27​.

    The limit can be found by using the inequality 0<n!3n​<2n27​.

    Fitting with a Function

    When a sequence {an​} can be fitted by a function f(x), we can apply L’Hopital’s Rule.

    Monotone Convergence Theorem

    By Monotone Convergence Theorem, every bounded monotonic sequence is convergent.

    A sequence is monotonic if it is either non-decreasing or non-increasing.

    For every n≥n0​, if an​≤an+1​, the sequence is non-decreasing.

    For every n≥n0​, if an​≥an+1​, the sequence is non-increasing.

    Non-decreasing if:

    • an+1​−an​≥0
    • an​an+1​​≥1 where an​>0
    • f′(x)≥0 where x≥n0​

    Non-increasing if:

    • an+1​−an​≤0
    • an​an+1​​≤1 where an​>0
    • f′(x)≤0 where x≥n0​

    A sequence {an​} is said to be bounded if m≤an​≤M for every n.

    M is an upper bound while m is a lower bound of the sequence.

    A bounded sequence may not always be convergent.

    #Series

    #Common Series

    Geometric Series

    Geometric sequence is a sequence {arn}n=0∞​ where a=0 is a constant.

    The common ratio r=an​an+1​​ is also a constant.

    n=0∑∞​arn=a+ar+ar2+...+arn
    where a=0 is convergent if ∣r∣<1 and its sum is 1−ra​

    When a geometric series does not start with n=0,

    n=K∑∞​arn=arK+arK+1+arK+2+...+arK+n

    n=K∑∞​(arK)rn=1−rarK​ ⟶ Sum=1−rFirst Term​

    n=0∑∞​arn=a+ar+ar2+...+arn
    where a=0 is divergent if ∣r∣>1

    Telescoping Series

    Telescoping series can be expressed in the form n=1∑∞​(an​−an+m​) for some m.

    Let SN​ be the partial sum of a telescoping series.

    As N→∞, we get n=1∑∞​(an​−an+m​)=N→∞lim​ n=1∑N​(an​−an+m​)=N→∞lim​SN​.

    For N>m>0, if the limit N→∞lim​an​=L exists, partial sum SN​=n=1∑m​an​−mL.

    Harmonic Series

    Harmonic series is n=1∑∞​n1​=1+21​+31​+...+n1​.

    Taking partial sums SN​ of the series,

    S1​=1

    S2​=1+21​

    S4​=1+21​+(31​+41​)

    S4​≥1+21​+(41​+41​)=1+2(21​)

    S8​=1+21​+(31​+41​)+(51​+61​+81​+81​)

    S8​≥1+21​+(41​+41​)+(81​+81​+81​+81​)=1+3(21​)

    Thus, S2n​≥1+2n​. Hence, n→∞lim​SN​=∞. The harmonic series is divergent.

    Alternating Series

    Alternating series n=1∑∞​(−1)n−1⋅bn​=b1​−b2​+b3​−b4​+... where bn​>0

    If n→∞lim​bn​=0 and bn+1​≤bn​ for all n (non-increasing), then the series converges.

    P-series

    A p-series n=1∑∞​np1​=1+2p1​+3p1​+...+np1​ converges if p>1, and diverges if p≤1.

    #Properties of Series

    Convergent Series

    If ∑an​ and ∑bn​ are convergent series, the following applies,

    ∑can​=c∑an​

    ∑(an​+bn​)=∑an​+∑bn​

    ∑(an​−bn​)=∑an​−∑bn​

    Divergent Series

    Every non-zero constant multiple of a divergent series is divergent.

    For example, a series c∑an​ is divergent if ∑an​ is divergent, regardless of c.

    If ∑an​ converges and ∑bn​ diverges, then ∑(an​±bn​) diverges.

    For example, the series n=1∑∞​(31​)n+n179​ is divergent since n=1∑∞​n179​ is divergent.

    #Divergence Test

    If a series n=0∑∞​an​ converges, then n→∞lim​an​=0.

    If n→∞lim​an​=0, it does not imply that the series is convergent.

    If n→∞lim​an​ does not exist or n→∞lim​an​=0, the series is divergent.

    #Integral Test

    Suppose an​=f(n) where f is a positive, continuous, decreasing function of x.
    If the integral ∫N∞​ f(x) dx converges, the series N∑∞​an​ converges.

    For example, f satisifies the conditions on the interval [1,∞), then if ∫1∞​ f(x) dx converges, the series converges. Integral converges if its limit c→∞lim​ ∫Nc​ f(x) dx exist.

    #Comparison Test

    Suppose that ∑an​ and ∑bn​ are two series with positive terms.

    If an​≤bn​ and ∑bn​ is convergent, then ∑an​ is also convergent.

    If an​≥bn​ and ∑bn​ is divergent, then ∑an​ is also divergent.

    Limit Comparison Test

    Suppose that an​>0 and bn​>0 for all n≥N, where N is some integer.

    If n→∞lim​bn​an​​>0 then both series either converge or diverge.

    If n→∞lim​bn​an​​=0 and ∑bn​ converges, then ∑an​ converges.

    If n→∞lim​bn​an​​=∞ and ∑bn​ diverges, then ∑an​ diverges.

    #Type of Convergence

    Aboslute Convergence

    A series ∑an​ is said to be absolutely convergent if the series of its absolute values
    ∑∣an​∣ is convergent. If an​≥0, then ∣an​∣=an​. Thus, if ∑an​ is a series with
    non-negative terms, then absolute convergence is the same as convergence.

    Conditional Convergence

    When ∑∣an​∣ diverges, then ∑an​ may either converge or diverge.

    If ∑an​ is convergent, then the series is conditionally convergent.

    If ∑an​ is divergent, then both ∑∣an​∣ and ∑an​ diverge.

    #Ratio Test

    If n→∞lim​​an​an+1​​​<1 , the series ∑an​ is absolutely convergent.

    If n→∞lim​​an​an+1​​​>1 or n→∞lim​​an​an+1​​​=∞, both ∑∣an​∣ and ∑an​ diverges.

    If n→∞lim​​an​an+1​​​=1, the ratio test is inconclusive.

    #Root Test

    If n→∞lim​n∣an​∣​<1 , the series ∑an​ is absolutely convergent.

    If n→∞lim​n∣an​∣​>1 or n→∞lim​n∣an​∣​=∞, both ∑∣an​∣ and ∑an​ diverges.

    If n→∞lim​n∣an​∣​=1, the ratio test is inconclusive.

    #Power Series

    A power series about x=0 is a series of the form:

    n=1∑∞​cn​xn=c0​+c1​x+c2​x2+...+cn​xn+...

    A power series about x=a is a series of the form:

    n=1∑∞​cn​xn=c0​+c1​(x−a)+c2​(x−a)2+...+cn​(x−a)n+...

    A power series can be differentiated/integrated term by term to obtain another series.

    #Radius of Convergence

    For a given power series, there are only three possibilities:

    • Converges absolutely for all x (Radius of convergence R=∞)
    • Converges only at one point x=a and diverges elsewhere (R=0)
    • Series converges if ∣x−a∣<R and diverges if ∣x−a∣>R

      where R is a positive real number

    The interval of convergence is the set of all values of x for which the series converges.

    • When R=∞, interval of convergence is (−∞,∞)
    • When R=0, interval of convergence is {a}
    • When R is a positive real number, (a−R,a+R) or [a−R,a+R]

      The brackets used is dependent on whether the series converges at that point.
      Open brackets if divergent and square brackets if convergent.

    #Taylor and Maclaurin Series

    Talyor series of a function f(x) at a is given by the power series:

    n=0∑∞​n!fn(a)​(x−a)n=f(a)+1!f1(a)​(x−a)1+2!f2(a)​(x−a)2+...+n!fn(a)​(x−a)n

    The Maclaurin series of a function f(x) is the power series centered at a=0:

    n=0∑∞​n!fn(0)​xn=f(0)+1!f1(0)​x1+2!f2(0)​x2+...+n!fn(0)​xn

    Taylor Remainder

    f(x)−Tn​(x)=Rn​(x) where Rn​ is the Taylor remainder

    f(x)−Tn​(x)=(n+1)!fn+1(c)​(x−a)n+1

    Rn​(x)=(n+1)!fn+1(c)​(x−a)n+1

    If n→∞lim​Rn​(x)=0, then f(x) is equal to the sum of its Taylor series.

    #Standard Power Series

    1−x1​=1+x+x2+x3+...

    ex=1+x+2!x2​+3!x3​+4!x4​+...

    ln(1+x)=x−2x2​+3x3​−4x4​+...

    sin x=x−3!x3​+5!x5​−7!x7​+...

    cos x=1−2!x2​+4!x4​−6!x6​+...

    #First Order Differential Equations

    #Differential Equations

    Separable Differential Equation

    A separable first-order differential equation is where expressions of x and y are separable.

    p(y) y′=q(x)

    p(y)⋅dxdy​=q(x)

    ∫p(y) dy=∫q(x) dx

    Alternative form of a separable first-order differential equation.

    dxdy​=f(x)⋅g(y)

    g(y)1​⋅dxdy​=f(x)

    ∫g(y)1​ dy=∫f(x) dx (if g(y)=0)

    Linear Differential Equation

    A first-order linear differetial equation can be written in the form,

    a(x)⋅dxdy​+b(x)⋅y=r(x)

    If the coefficient of dxdy​=1, the equation is in standard form.

    To solve linear equations, reduce the equation to its standard form.

    dxdy​+P(x)⋅y=Q(x)

    v(x)⋅dxdy​+P(x)v(x)⋅y=v(x)Q(x) (Multiplying by v)

    dxd​[v(x)⋅y]=v(x)Q(x)

    v(x)⋅y=∫v(x)Q(x) dx (Integrating with respect to x)

    y=v(x)1​∫v(x)Q(x) dx (where v is the integrating factor)

    dxd​ vy=vdxdy​+Pvy

    vdxdy​+ydxdv​=vdxdy​+Pvy

    dxdv​=Pv

    ∫v1​ dv=∫P dx

    v=e ∫P dx

    where v(x) is the integrating factor

    #Reduction to First O.D.E.

    Missing y-variable

    Suppose y is missing from a differential equation, dx2d2y​=x1​(dxdy​+x2cosx).

    The derivatives can be substituted with z=dxdy​ and z′=dx2d2y​.

    This reduces the O.D.E. to z′=x1​(z+x2cos).

    The equation can be solved as a linear equation.

    Since z=dxdy​, the solution needs to be integrated again to obtain an expression for y.

    Missing x-variable

    Suppose x is missing from a differential equation, dx2d2y​=−1−y2​(dxdy​)2.

    Let z=dxdy​ and z′=dxd​(dxdy​)=(dyd​⋅dxdy​)(dxdy​)=dydz​⋅z.

    This reduces the O.D.E to zdydz​=(−1−y2​)z2.

    The equation can be solved as a linear equation.

    #Types of Differential Equations

    Homogeneous Differential Equation

    A function f(x,y) is homogeneous if f(tx,ty) can be reduced back to f(x,y).

    For a homogeneous equation, x and y can be replaced with a single variable V,
    where V=xy​. The function then becomes y=Vx where dxdy​=xdxdV​+V.
    Substitute the new variable and its derivative into the equation and solve.

    Bernoulli Differential Equation

    A bernoulli equation is in the form,

    dxdy​+p(x)⋅y=q(x)⋅yα

    If α=0, it becomes a linear equation.
    If     α=1, the equation is separable and linear.

    Dividing both sides of the equation by yα,

    y−αdxdy​+y1−α⋅p(x)=q(x)

    Let u=y1−α.

    dxdu​=dydu​⋅dxdy​

    dxdu​=(1−α)y−αdxdy​

    y−αdxdy​=1−α1​dxdu​

    Substituting back into the equation,

    1−α1​dxdu​+u⋅p(x)=q(x)

    dxdu​+(1−α)u⋅p(x)=(1−α)⋅q(x)

    The equation can be rearranged into standard form and solved.

    Exact Differential Equation

    For a differential equation in the form M(x,y) dx+N(x,y) dy=0,
    it is exact if there exist a function u(x,y) for which ∂x∂u​=M and ∂y∂u​=N.

    The function u(x,y) is thus the potential function (general solution).

    A differential equation is exact if and only if ∂y∂M​=∂x∂N​.

    A non-exact equation can be transformed to an exact equation by multiplying
    it with a non-zero function I(x,y), such that the equation becomes,

    I(x,y)M(x,y) dx+I(x,y)N(x,y) dy=0

    ∂y∂​ I(x,y)M(x,y)=∂x∂​ I(x,y)N(x,y)

    where I(x,y) is the integrating factor

    #Second Order Differential Equations

    #Homogeneous Linear Differential Equation

    A homogeneous linear differential equation with constant coefficients is in the form,

    adx2d2y​+bdxdy​+cy=0 where the coefficients are real constants

    The coefficients form a quadratic equation called the characteristic equation. Solving
    the characteristic equation gives the general solution of the differential equation.

    aλ2+bλ+c=0

    λ=2a−b±b2−4ac​​

    If b2−4ac>0, then the quadratic equation has two distinct real roots.

    If b2−4ac=0, then the quadratic equation has a repeating real root.

    If b2−4ac<0, then the quadratic equation has two complex conjugate roots.

    Real & Distinct Rootsy=c1​eλ1​x+c2​eλ2​x
    Repeating Rootsy=c1​eλ0​x+c2​xeλ0​x
    Complex Rootsy=eαx(c1​sinβx+c2​cosβx) where α is real, β is complex

    #Non-Homogeneous Linear Differential Equation

    A non-homogeneous linear differential equation is in the form,

    adx2d2y​+bdxdy​+cy=F(x) where F(x) is continuous on interval I

    The associated homogeneous equation is in the form,

    adx2d2y​+bdxdy​+cy=0

    Let yh​ be the general solution to the associated homogeneous equation.

    Let yp​ be a particular solution to the non-homogeneous equation.

    Thus, the general solution is y=yh​+yp​.

    Method of Undetermined Coefficients

    F(x) must contain the following expressions for this method:

    • Polynomials
    • Consines or sines
    • Exponential function
    • Sums or products of the above

    The expressions stated above have derivatives (are differentiable).

    Step 1: Choose a form of yp​ similar to an expression in F(x)

    Step 2: Check whether yp​ is the same solution as yh​

    Step 3: Differentiate yp​ and substitute into non-homogeneous equation

    Method of Variation of Parameters

    Suppose the general solution to the associated homogeneous equation is,

    yh​=c1​y1​+c2​y2​

    Replacing the coefficients c1​ and c2​ with u1​ and u2​ (functions of x),

    yp​=u1​y1​+u2​y2​

    Impose the condition u1′​y1​+u2′​y2​=0.

    Differentiate yp​ to obtain expressions for yp′​ and yp′′​.

    Substitute yp​, yp′​ and yp′′​ into the non-homogeneous equation.

    The two simultaneous equations are then,

    u1′​y1​+u2′​y2​=0

    yp′′​+yp′​+yp​=F(x)
